name: Methamphetamine
mechanisms: Monoamine releaser (dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin; from a narrative review, draft)
Thought to act on VMAT2 and the membrane transporters (from a narrative review, draft)

dates.last_search: 2026-10-14 (Crossref layer only; PubMed, Cochrane and citation searches not yet run)

authors.name: Claude (Anthropic)
authors.role: AI co-editor: first-pass extraction, appraisal and drafting

at_a_glance.mechanism_line: A substituted amphetamine that, as described in a narrative review (section 3), raises extracellular dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin, apparently by moving them out of storage vesicles and reversing their transporters; the mechanism is not completely understood.
at_a_glance.legal_summary: Schedule II of the UN Convention on Psychotropic Substances (1971), which binds the countries party to it. Class A in the United Kingdom; Schedule II in the United States, where a prescription product is approved for ADHD; Schedule I in Canada; no EU-level schedule, as member states classify drugs nationally. In Greece it is listed in Table Γ΄ of the national drug tables (Ministry of Health consolidated list, June 2026); the Australian entry is not yet confirmed from the official text (section 13). Checked against official texts on 16 October 2026; draft until the senior author's check.

sections.title: Pharmacology
sections.no_evidence_note: Not yet searched: metabolism and active metabolites, bioavailability by route, pharmacogenetics, and the mechanisms of drug–drug interactions. The pharmacokinetic studies on the reading list have not yet been read.

sections.title: Neuroscience
sections.no_evidence_note: Not yet covered: dopamine D2/3 receptor availability and stimulant-induced dopamine release (reported in a meta-analysis and a review already cited in this section), the serotonin transporter and other markers outside the dopamine system, white-matter (diffusion) imaging, magnetic resonance spectroscopy, functional MRI and EEG, the acute effects of a dose on the brain, and animal neurotoxicity studies beyond those summarized in the contested question. Their absence here is not evidence of no effect.

sections.title: Acute risks
sections.no_evidence_note: Not yet covered: pregnancy and newborn outcomes, people with heart disease or a psychiatric history, adolescents, and interactions. Papers on pregnancy are on the reading list and have not been read.

sections.title: Routes of administration and practical risk reduction
sections.no_evidence_note: Not written yet. This section will be added by the senior author after a legal review, to the same citation standard as every other section.

sections.title: Long-term effects
sections.no_evidence_note: Not yet covered: cardiovascular disease (including cardiomyopathy), stroke, dental disease and infections such as HIV and hepatitis. Papers are on the reading list and have not been read; their absence here is not evidence of no harm. Treatment of methamphetamine psychosis is in section 12.

sections.title: Harm-reduction interventions
sections.no_evidence_note: Not written yet. The papers to read are on the reading list: experiences of overdose, use alongside opioids, fentanyl contamination, safer-smoking kits, pipe sharing and prescribed stimulants. Drug-checking data for methamphetamine have not yet been searched.

sections.title: Treatment and therapeutic research
sections.no_evidence_note: Five questions have been appraised so far, all on medicines: one trial of naltrexone with bupropion; two trials of mirtazapine from one team; a meta-analysis of psychostimulant medicines (bupropion, modafinil, methylphenidate, dexamphetamine) for the use disorder; a meta-analysis of medicines for withdrawal; and antipsychotic treatment of psychosis, known so far only from narrative reviews. Still on the reading list and not yet read: systematic reviews of medicines for the use disorder, including one of mirtazapine, of contingency management and of other psychosocial treatments, and trials of contingency management and the Matrix Model, and a systematic review of antipsychotics for methamphetamine psychosis; one further systematic review of medicines has been read but is not yet used in a claim. No psychosocial treatment is covered yet, and this section does not yet show which treatments have the strongest evidence.

sections.title: Research gaps
sections.no_evidence_note: The priority questions are the editors' selection, drawn from the review of all claims (review round 1); the lists below them are generated from the debate boxes, the very-low-certainty claims and the study cards.

priority_questions.question: How common are psychotic symptoms among people who use meth occasionally, and at what frequency of use does the risk rise?
priority_questions.needs: Community cohorts with biologically checked use and repeated assessments of psychotic symptoms.

priority_questions.question: Does meth psychosis lead to a lasting psychotic illness, or reveal a vulnerability that was already there?
priority_questions.needs: First-episode cohorts with early measures of vulnerability, follow-up after verified abstinence, and comparison groups who use other drugs.

priority_questions.question: Does meth use increase violence within the same person, apart from psychosis?
priority_questions.needs: Within-person cohorts with outcomes taken from records rather than self-report alone.

priority_questions.question: Are the links with depression and suicidal behaviour specific to meth, or shared with drug use in general?
priority_questions.needs: Cohorts comparing people who use meth with people who use other drugs, with diagnostic interviews.

priority_questions.question: How much of the excess mortality is due to meth itself?
priority_questions.needs: Register cohorts with comparison groups matched on injecting, other drug use and social disadvantage.

priority_questions.question: Does any treatment produce lasting reductions in use?
priority_questions.needs: Independent replication of the medication trials, in other populations and with follow-up after treatment ends (one mirtazapine trial reported fewer positive urine tests 12 weeks after medication stopped), and comparison with contingency management.

sections.not_yet_covered: Cardiovascular disease (including cardiomyopathy), stroke, dental disease and other physical harms; pregnancy and newborn outcomes; infections such as HIV and hepatitis; brain-imaging measures other than the dopamine transporter, VMAT2, glucose metabolism and grey matter (dopamine receptors and release, serotonin, white matter, functional imaging); acute risks for adolescents and for people with heart disease or a psychiatric history; drug interactions, metabolism and active metabolites, bioavailability by route and pharmacogenetics; the methamphetamine-specific chance of developing a use disorder (section 8 gives only a 1990–1992 figure for stimulants grouped); drug-checking data and harm-reduction interventions; contingency management and other treatments; and European and Greek data; tolerance with repeated use, how long it takes to return to baseline after stopping, and cross-tolerance with other stimulants (a standard question since protocol 0.2.6; papers are being listed).

changelog.change: Prototype monograph: 13 draft claims, 19 first-pass study cards, 22 metadata-verified references. No excerpt verified yet.

Claims rebuilt from full texts: 10 papers read from the PDFs the senior author saved and 22 read in full in PubMed Central or on the publisher's free site. 32 claims (19 new), each with page- or section-located evidence anchors; the combined 'brain damage' debate split into two (dopamine neurons; cognition); GRADE arithmetic checked by the validator; certainty lowered where full texts showed problems the abstracts did not (Parkinson's disease, dopamine-transporter recovery).

Sections 2 (identity) and 13 (legal status) filled from official sources (draft, 19 and 8 sources); the at-a-glance legal line corrected: the 1971 Convention binds its parties, not all UN member states.

Review round 1 (an independent methodologist review of all 32 claims in three groups) adjudicated against the sources: 31 claims revised and 1 added (mechanism, section 3). Certainty lowered where upgrades broke METHODS §6.3 (within-person psychosis cohort and US trends: moderate → low; mortality kept at low with the large-effect upgrade and the inconsistency downgrade both removed); same-laboratory pairs relabelled 'replicated by the same team'; five claims resting only on narrative reviews held at draft; antipsychotic treatment moved to section 12; at-a-glance box re-selected by a stated rule and shown with each claim's rating; notes added where harms and treatments are not yet covered; last search date stated.

Nine study cards re-checked in adjudication round 1b merged (19 cards now checked by a second AI reader); a second blind reading of the five narrative reviews recorded on each card, with the domains where the two readers differ left to the senior author; a reporting issue added to London et al. (2015) on the uncorrected threshold of its Figure 1. The abstinence and cognition claim is now ai-anchored after a targeted check of its last anchor. Person-first wording throughout the study cards. Legal status: Greece row filled from the Ministry of Health's consolidated tables (Table Γ΄, item 52), still awaiting the senior author's check. At a glance: the psychosis-course question, which rests only on narrative reviews, replaced among the largest uncertainties by whether thinking improves with abstinence (METHODS §6.3; methods audit M16); the mechanism line now says it is described second-hand; the legal summary gives the Greek table.

Review round 2: three independent methodologists reviewed all claims with the saved full texts open, and each of their 124 findings was adjudicated against the source (data/verification/review2/adjudication/). One certainty change: suicidal thoughts and attempts lowered from low to very low (risk of bias: four cross-sectional studies in selected emergency, justice and treatment samples). Many claims now report results in both directions where the earlier text kept only one (abstinence and thinking; transporter recovery; brain glucose by sex), name the samples behind pooled estimates (psychosis, suicidality), separate the certainty of a direction from that of a size (dopamine transporter), and say when a figure is second-hand; figures read only from an abstract were removed from the base-rate claim. 58 anchors were added from the saved full texts; they are located, not yet checked, so ten claims are back to metadata-verified until a second reader checks them. Two staged treatment claims entered section 12 (bupropion or modafinil; medicines for withdrawal), with their eleven study cards; the mirtazapine claim waits for a complete reference record of its first trial. The sibling brain-structure claim moved to section 4, the cognition causal question is shown under Cognition in section 9 as well as in section 14, section 4 now says what it does not cover, the header's mechanism tags say they come from a narrative review, and the research-gaps summary lists the gaps the sections declare. Person-first wording in the anchors and reasoning.

An independent reader checked 63 anchors at the stated place in the saved full texts (the 55 located anchors whose sources are saved, including those added in review round 2, and 8 anchors edited in that round): 55 confirmed, 7 corrected (wording narrowed or hedges restored; no number was wrong) and 1 relocated (data/verification/targeted-2026-10-16b/). 13 claims now have every anchor checked by a second reader (ai-anchored), up from one; the remaining located anchors need sources that are not saved yet.
Wording of the notes on sections not yet written (no claim changed): plain wording for sections 7 and 11; internal reading-list numbers removed from the notes.

Mirtazapine claim added to section 12 (two trials from one team, low certainty), now that the first trial's reference record is complete (author list from PubMed Central); section 12's note and research question 6 updated to match.

New claim on crime (McKetin et al., 2020), the violence claim's relation and status updated, and the siblings claim corrected from the Ersche et al. (2012) supplement (batch 3c: first reader AI reader 29, second reader AI reader 33, adjudicator AI reader 37).

The contested answer on excited delirium (cl_gen_deaths_excited_delirium, deaths round of 1 November, completed by ChatGPT's readers and merged on 10 November) added to section 14, as it is asked on this drug's page.
